verses.text: Come near, you nations, to hear! Listen, you peoples. Let the earth and all it contains hear; the world, and everything that comes from it.
For Yahweh is enraged against all the nations, and angry with all their armies. He has utterly destroyed them. He has given them over for slaughter.
Their slain will also be cast out, and the stench of their dead bodies will come up; and the mountains will melt in their blood.
All of the army of the sky will be dissolved. The sky will be rolled up like a scroll, and all its armies will fade away, as a leaf fades from off a vine or a fig tree.
For my sword has drunk its fill in the sky. Behold, it will come down on Edom, and on the people of my curse, for judgment.

Yahweh’s sword is filled with blood. It is covered with fat, with the blood of lambs and goats, with the fat of the kidneys of rams; for Yahweh has a sacrifice in Bozrah, And a great slaughter in the land of Edom.
The wild oxen will come down with them, and the young bulls with the mighty bulls; and their land will be drunken with blood, and their dust made greasy with fat.
For Yahweh has a day of vengeance, a year of recompense for the cause of Zion.
Its streams will be turned into pitch, its dust into sulfur, And its land will become burning pitch.
It won’t be quenched night nor day. Its smoke will go up forever. From generation to generation, it will lie waste. No one will pass through it forever and ever.
But the pelican and the porcupine will possess it. The owl and the raven will dwell in it. He will stretch the line of confusion over it, and the plumb line of emptiness.
They shall call its nobles to the kingdom, but none shall be there; and all its princes shall be nothing.
Thorns will come up in its palaces, nettles and thistles in its fortresses; and it will be a habitation of jackals, a court for ostriches.
The wild animals of the desert will meet with the wolves, and the wild goat will cry to his fellow. Yes, the night creature  shall settle there, and shall find herself a place of rest.
The arrow snake will make her nest there, and lay, hatch, and gather under her shade. Yes, the kites will be gathered there, every one with her mate.
Search in the book of Yahweh, and read: not one of these will be missing. none will lack her mate. For my mouth has commanded, and his Spirit has gathered them.
He has cast the lot for them, and his hand has divided it to them with a measuring line. They shall possess it forever. From generation to generation they will dwell in it.

footnotes.content: Isaiah calls all creation to witness—nations, peoples, earth itself. There's a grandeur in how the Lord speaks: what He has to say concerns everyone, from the greatest kingdoms down to the dust beneath our feet. Listen first, with your whole heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here we see the Lord's wrath is real and thorough—not a passing mood, but a settled judgment against all who have set their armies against Him and His people. Yet even in anger, He acts with perfect justice; He does not rage like men do.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The imagery is stark and terrible: death is displayed, not hidden. The mountains themselves seem to witness the gore—a reversal of any comfort nature might offer. This is what rebellion against the Almighty truly costs.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "All the army of the sky will be dissolved… rolled up like a scroll." This imagery echoes into later Scripture—what Isaiah foresees, John sees at last in Revelation. The heavens themselves acknowledge the coming judgment and the sovereignty of the One who will remake all things.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Edom, the people of Esau—"people of my curse"—falls under the Lord's judgment. The sword of the Lord is not made by human hands, yet it descends with perfect aim. What seemed settled, distant, or forgotten by men is remembered and addressed by God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The language of "sacrifice" and "slaughter" in Bozrah is a real place—the fortress of Edom. Isaiah speaks as a prophet who knows the geography of judgment, making the threat concrete and unavoidable, not vague or distant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even the animals—wild oxen and bulls—become caught up in the judgment, their strength useless against the tide. In moments of God's judgment, nothing we build or breed can save us; only His mercy can.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The Lord has a day of vengeance, a year of recompense for the cause of Zion." Here is the deep comfort: the Lord does not forget His people's suffering, nor does He overlook the cause of His own. Justice delayed is not justice denied.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The land is transformed into something uninhabitable—pitch, sulfur, burning. This is not a gentle pruning but a radical emptying, a complete reversal of fruitfulness. Some judgments remake the land itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "It won't be quenched night nor day." The permanence of desolation is absolute—generation after generation inherit emptiness. This teaches us the weight of rebellion: some consequences stretch so far into the future that we can barely see the end.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pelican, porcupine, owl, raven—creatures of waste and solitude inherit what was once a kingdom. Where grandeur stood, only loneliness remains. The Lord's "plumb line of emptiness" is a strange kind of building tool, but it measures faithfully.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The nobles and princes are called to a kingdom that no longer exists—a mockery of their former power. When we build on anything but the Rock, even our thrones become ghost halls. Empty glory is the truest emptiness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Thorns rise where palaces once stood; jackals court in where armies once marched. This reversal—wilderness reclaiming what man built—reminds us that creation itself speaks against pride. The earth remembers what the Lord intends.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wild animals meet and dwell together in the desolation—a strange fellowship of creatures who find rest only in ruin. There is something almost peaceful in the image, yet it is desolation speaking. The creatures are not content; they are displaced.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The arrow snake makes her nest and the kites gather—even in waste, life finds its own rhythm, its own shelter. Yet this life is not the flourishing the land once knew; it is survival stripped to its simplest form.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Search in the book of Yahweh, and read." Isaiah commands us to consult the Lord's own book, His Spirit-gathered assembly of all these creatures and their coming destiny. This is an invitation to trust Scripture itself—nothing is left to chance or forgotten.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Looking back from where we stand, readers today hear an echo in this strange promise: the humble creatures inherit the earth, and what was measured out for waste endures forever. In a strange way, we see that even in judgment, the Lord's order persists—and mercy, quieter than thunder, reserves a future.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
